name: Dev Raman
case_formulation: Dev (Devendra) Raman, 34, he/him, backend software engineer at Larkspur (patient-records software). ADHD diagnosed at 30 after his partner Mei pushed him to get assessed: poor task initiation, time blindness ('now and not now'), procrastination that flips into late-night hyperfocus on side projects (a bus-times app, a synth plugin) followed by crashes. Father, a retired civil engineer, read his school reports aloud at the dinner table ending with 'if you just applied yourself', checked his homework every Sunday with a red pen while standing behind his chair, exhaled audibly before every verdict, and skipped his graduation over a 2:1. As a boy Dev coped by switching off (lying under his desk for hours). Mother (Amma) covered for him and fixed things; partner Mei, a hospital pharmacist, now runs all the household bills and admin. Older sister Kavya, a cardiologist, is the favoured achiever. Core belief: 'I'm lazy and a fraud, and any criticism proves it.' Rules: hide, look busy, always be visibly present, never be caught not knowing. Trigger pattern: evaluation of his work (code review, check-ins) leads to shame and shutdown or avoidance. He was let go from his previous job at Kestrel on Friday 26 July 2024 and spent his first year at Larkspur always last out of the building. Manager Ruth is fair and arranged his accommodations (written tickets, headphones); by late June he privately calls her 'the Captain'. Started a long-acting stimulant in early May 2026, it clearly helped, stopped it in mid-June because of appetite loss and insomnia. Bouldering with colleague Priya quieted his mind in May; his membership lapsed by late June. In June he becomes buddy to an intern, Tobi, and notices he hears his father's harsh version of feedback first. Father has a knee replacement in July; father's health is not clinically relevant.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi Dev, welcome. Make yourself comfortable. What made you decide to come in?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Honestly? Mei, my partner, booked it and sent me the confirmation with three exclamation marks. Which is fair, I've been saying I'd do this for about a year. I'm a software engineer, I'm thirty-four, and I'm very good at my job about forty percent of the time. The other sixty I'm hiding.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hiding how?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Looking busy. Tabs open. I'll have a ticket that should take two hours and I'll circle it for three days, then do it at one in the morning in a kind of fever, and it'll be good, and I'll still feel like a fraud. Rinse and repeat.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Where do you work?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Larkspur. We make patient-records software for clinics, I'm on the backend team. My manager, Ruth, is honestly the best manager I've had. When I asked if requests could come as written tickets instead of people turning up at my desk, she just said sure, and made it team policy so I wasn't the odd one out. She fought for my headphones budget. Which means I'm terrified of letting her down, obviously.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: So she's been on your side, and that raises the stakes.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Exactly. With a bad manager I'd at least have someone to blame. Anyway. It's a good job, good people. I just keep waiting for someone to notice I'm making it up as I go along.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What would they notice, do you think?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: That I'm not a real adult? Like, at home, Mei does all the bills. Council tax, the energy people, the water, everything. The one year I was in charge we got a final demand, and she quietly took it all over and never mentioned it again. She has a system. I have vibes.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: (smiles) Vibes. How does it feel that she carries all that?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Relief, mostly. Some guilt. She works shifts at the hospital pharmacy, she's knackered, and she still does my admin. I'd be lost without her. I'd be living in a tent made of unopened envelopes.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: You mentioned feeling like a fraud. Where do you think that comes from?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Oh, we're doing childhood already? Okay. My father's a civil engineer, bridges, a very exact man. School reports came home twice a year and he'd read them out at the dinner table, line by line, like evidence in a trial. 'Devendra is bright, but.' There was always a but. Then he'd put the report down and say, if you just applied yourself. Every single time.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Every single time.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Like a catchphrase. Kavya, my sister, got hers read out too, but hers didn't have a 'but' in them. She's a cardiologist now, so. Anyway, he's retired. He does sudoku and writes letters to the council about potholes. He's fine. We're fine.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: We're fine. I noticed that came out quite quickly.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: (laughs) Did it? I've had thirty-four years of practice. Can we talk about something else for a bit? I cycled here and a delivery van nearly took me out, so my heart's still going.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Of course. What would be most useful to focus on, day to day?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: The procrastination, probably. I got diagnosed with ADHD at thirty, after Mei found my keys in the fridge for the second time and made me book an assessment. So I've got the vocabulary now. Executive dysfunction, task initiation, all of it. Having the words didn't make it go away. Before that I just thought I was lazy and clever, in that order.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Lazy and clever. That sounds like a verdict you got from somewhere.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yeah, okay, I heard it. Point taken. I'm also up till two most nights on side projects. Right now it's an app that tells you whether the number fourteen bus is lying about being five minutes away. Nobody asked for it. I love it.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: We'll come back to all of that. Same time in two weeks?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yes. I'll put it in my calendar, and then Mei will put it in hers, which is the one that actually counts.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Good to see you, Dev. How have the last two weeks been?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Eventful. I started medication, finally. The GP sorted the shared-care paperwork and I'm on a stimulant, the long-acting kind, lowest dose to begin with. Eight days in. The first morning I cleaned the oven, which is apparently a cliché. Too early to tell anything.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How are you finding it so far?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Weird. Good weird, I think. My mouth's dry all the time and I'm drinking a lot of water. Mei's put a sticky note on the fridge that says EAT LUNCH, DEVENDRA. She only uses my full name in capitals.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: She's looking out for you.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: She is. Meanwhile my dad's knee is finally getting done, he's on the list for July. He's furious about it, like the knee's being insubordinate. Amma's driving him to every appointment and texting me updates with a lot of prayer-hands emojis.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How do you feel about his surgery?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Fine? He'll be fine. It's strange picturing him in a hospital gown, though. He was always so upright. Sundays he'd go through my homework at the kitchen table with a red pen, standing behind my chair, ticking and crossing and not saying a word. I can still hear the nib. Anyway. He's sixty-eight. Bodies go.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: You can still hear it.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Funny what sticks. After report nights I used to go up to my room and lie on the carpet under my desk. Not crying, not even sulking. Just switched off, sometimes for hours. Amma would leave a plate outside the door and knock once.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Switched off. A way of getting through it.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I guess. Amma was the one who made things okay, generally. She signed permission slips I'd forgotten, found my PE kit, finished a volcano project at midnight once so it'd be there in the morning. Dad never knew half of it. She was basically my handler.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Your handler. That's quite a job description.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: She'd still do it now if I let her. Before Larkspur I was at Kestrel, a logistics startup, and when they let me go, two years ago this July, the twenty-sixth, a Friday, Amma was the first person I rang. Security walked me out with a cardboard box like in a film. I didn't tell my father for four months.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Four months is a long time to hold something like that.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I had Amma, so it wasn't nothing. Anyway. I've been very productive in other areas. On Sunday I wrote a nine-hundred-word review of a ramen place on the neighbourhood food site instead of doing a ticket. With subheadings. The broth deserved it.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: (laughs) The broth deserved it. Do you notice when the switch to side tasks happens?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Always right before the real thing. It's like my brain sees the task and goes, have you considered ramen? And I go, well, I have now.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What happens in your body just before you switch?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: A sort of fizz in my chest. Like dread, but caffeinated. Priya at work keeps telling me to come bouldering with her, she says it's 'dread for your hands instead'. I said maybe. I'm a maybe person.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Maybe is a start. What would turn it into a yes?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Someone physically collecting me from the flat so I can't bail. Which she has threatened to do. She's very persistent for someone so small.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: She sounds like a good friend. Let's stop there. Notice the fizz this week, if you can.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Homework. Great. (laughs) No, I'll try. I'll write it in a note on my phone that I will never open again.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi Dev. How's the fortnight been?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Okay, plot twist, I've been climbing. Priya actually turned up at my door and drove me to the bouldering place by the canal. I've been three times since. I'm terrible at it. But for an hour my brain is completely quiet. You can't think about anything when you're hanging off a wall by your fingertips. And I sleep like a stone after.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Completely quiet. That's not nothing.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It's really not. And the meds are kind of wild. It's like someone turned the radio down in the next room. I wrote a design doc start to finish in one sitting on Thursday. I nearly cried. I also forgot to eat until seven at night, so, swings and roundabouts.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Two things helping at the same time.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Don't jinx it. (laughs) Mei's pleased. She says I'm less of a weather system. We had her parents over for dinner on Saturday and I didn't disappear into my phone once.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What was that like?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Her dad asked about work and I actually answered in full sentences. Usually I go vague, because I'm scared of the follow-up question. Her parents are lovely. They're retired teachers, they live for follow-up questions.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: And how are things at work?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Better. I'm doing more code reviews for other people, which I actually love. It's like a puzzle where I'm not the one being solved. Ruth suggested a timer thing, twenty-five minutes on, five off. I lasted a day. The alarm went, I snoozed it and kept reading about lighthouses.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: The timer didn't stick.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Nothing that relies on future-me sticks. Mei says I live in two tenses, now and not now, and not-now doesn't really exist. I'll set a reminder, and when it goes off I genuinely think, who is this for? Some stranger's problem.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Some stranger's problem. That's a vivid way to put it.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: My sister Kavya's the total opposite. She's got her kids' birthday parties planned to 2030. I love her, but family holidays with her are like a military operation. There's a laminated itinerary.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How are you feeling about your dad's operation?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It's in July. He's being stoic about it, very him. I'll go and sit with him, obviously. Even though he didn't come to my graduation. I got a two-one and he said he'd have come for a first. Amma and Kavya came and took about a hundred photos. He said well done on the phone that night, like a receptionist.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Like a receptionist. That must have stung.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It's fine. It was twelve years ago. (pause) Okay, it's not totally fine. Can we talk about something lighter? I've been building a synth plugin at night. It makes everything sound like it's underwater.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What draws you to it?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Nobody's waiting for it. No deadline, no one to disappoint. I can be bad at it in private. I was up till half three on Friday with it and it was the best night of my week.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Being bad at something in private sounds like a relief.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Total relief. Mei says it's the only hobby I've ever finished, except I haven't finished it, so she's being generous.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: We're near time. How's sleep been since the medication?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Fine so far. A bit wired till midnight, but I'm a night owl anyway, so honestly, who can tell.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Let's keep an eye on it. See you in two weeks.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: See you. I'll bring a plugin demo. You'll hate it, it's mostly whale noises and static.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi Dev. How are you doing?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Tired, in a good way? Also, we've got a new intern on the team, Tobi, and Ruth's asked me to be his buddy, which is terrifying. He's twenty-two and very earnest and he writes down things I say. Nobody should be writing down things I say.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What feels terrifying about it?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: What if I'm the bad example? He'll copy my habits. He'll start doing his tickets at one in the morning and think that's just what engineers do.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What would you want him to take from you?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: That it's okay not to know things. Which I don't believe myself, so that'll be very convincing.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: You might teach it before you believe it. Where did you learn that not knowing wasn't okay?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: The usual place. The words weren't even the worst bit, though. It was before the words. He'd hold the report and breathe out through his nose, this long slow exhale, and lay it face down next to his plate. Then you knew. Kavya says she still can't stand it when people do that in meetings.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: The exhale before the verdict.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yeah. I can do a pretty good impression. I won't. (laughs) Mei's had a migraine since Friday, by the way, so I've been on dark-room duty. Bringing her toast and not talking. I'm good at not talking.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: You're good at looking after her.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: When it's concrete. Toast, water, curtains. The abstract stuff she does. I got us tickets to a gig in August, that's my contribution to the summer.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How are your working hours at the moment?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Reasonable, for me. When I first started at Larkspur I was the last one out of the building for about a year. No one asked me to. I just had this idea that if I was always visibly there, they couldn't do a Kestrel on me again. The cleaners knew my name and my coffee order.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: So they couldn't do it to you again.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Mei used to bring dinner to my desk, like a zookeeper. Now I'm mostly home by six, which she counts as a personal victory. She's put it on the calendar.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It sounds like something has eased.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Some things. Dad's blood pressure is up before the surgery, so they might postpone, and he's taking it out on Amma by reorganising the garage. That's his stress mode. Moving heavy things in silence.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Moving heavy things in silence. Does that sound at all familiar?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: (laughs) Rude. Accurate, but rude. Mei says I'm my father's son when I spend three hours tidying the cables behind the TV instead of having a conversation.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What conversation were you avoiding?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Whether we do Diwali at Kavya's or with her parents. It's months away. I said let's decide later. She said that's what you always say, which is also accurate and also rude.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: We'll keep an eye on the avoiding. Anything else before we stop?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Tobi's first code review is Thursday. I'm reviewing his, I mean, not the other way round. Pray for him.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: I suspect you'll be kinder than you fear.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: I'll try. I'll be nicer to him than I am to myself, anyway, which is a low bar, but it's a bar.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi Dev. How have things been?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: So, I stopped the meds. About ten days ago. I wasn't hungry till nine at night, I'd lost weight I didn't have to lose, and I was lying awake till three with my heart going. The GP said we could try a different one or a lower dose, and I said let me have a break first. So I'm on a break.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That sounds like a reasonable call given the side effects. How do you feel about it?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Like I failed the medication exam. Which I know isn't a thing. Mei says I didn't fail anything, the pill failed me. She's very pro-me.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: She is. How's the rest of life?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Bit flat. I haven't been to the wall in about a month. My membership ran out, and I keep meaning to renew it, and then it's eleven at night and I'm on the sofa. Priya's stopped asking, which is somehow worse than her asking.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: It sounds like two supports have dropped away at once.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: When you say it like that. Work's okay, at least. The Captain's been on holiday, so it's been calm. Sorry, the Captain is Ruth, my manager. Priya and I started calling her that because she says 'all hands' on every call and she steers a meeting like a ship through rocks. Affectionately. Mostly affectionately.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: (smiles) Mostly affectionately.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: She'd probably find it funny. She's got a sense of humour under the clipboard. Anyway, Tobi's code review went fine. I wrote everything as questions, not statements. He thanked me. Then I went home and lay down for an hour, it took that much out of me.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Being gentle cost you something.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It's like translating. I hear the harsh version first, in my head, word for word, and then I rewrite it into the human version before it goes out. It takes ages. I don't think most people have to do that.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Whose voice is the harsh version?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: You know whose. (pause) Speaking of. Dad's surgery is booked for the fourteenth of July. Kavya's taking the first two weeks, I'm doing the weekend after that. Amma's made a rota. It's laminated.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How do you feel about doing your part?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Fine. Practical. I'll take my laptop in case I get bored, which I will. Amma will feed me every forty minutes. I'll come back three kilos heavier, which after the meds is probably the plan.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: (smiles) That sounds like Amma.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Very Amma. Meanwhile I've gone a bit feral at night. Off the meds, the side projects are back with a vengeance. On Saturday I was up till four rewriting the bus app in a different language, for no reason at all. Mei found me at dawn and said I looked haunted.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What are those late nights like?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Honestly? Great while it's happening. Then terrible. Sunday was a write-off. I couldn't do anything, I just lay on the sofa feeling like burnt toast.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: A crash after the high.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yeah. Mei calls it my hangover without the fun part. She's not wrong. She's rarely wrong, it's very annoying.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Can we think about the next fortnight? What's one small thing within reach?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Renewing the membership. I know. I know. I'll do it tonight. (pause) I probably won't do it tonight.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Probably won't is honest. We'll see where you are in two weeks.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Thanks. Sorry I was a bit flat today. Next time I'll bring jokes, or at least the whale noises.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Hi Dev. How's the last fortnight been?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Quiet, mostly. The Captain's been off at some half-year planning thing for a week, so nobody's been steering and the team's sort of drifted. I've been working nine till six like a functional person. Mostly.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Nine till six. How has that felt?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Strange. Like wearing someone else's shoes. Good shoes, but I keep checking they're still on.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What else has been going on?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Mei's sister had a baby, so Mei's flying out to stay with them for a bit later in the summer. I'm really happy for them. I bought the baby a onesie with a cassette tape on it. Mei says it's for me, not the baby.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: (laughs) What else did Mei say?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: That I need to get a spare key cut before she goes, because last time she went away I locked myself out twice. Which, fair. I've written KEY on my hand. It's already fading.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How are things with your dad, with the surgery coming up?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It's next week. Dad rang me, which he never does, to ask if I could look at his printer. That's how he asks for company. We spent an hour on a printer that turned out to be unplugged.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: That's quite a tender way of asking.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yeah. He's sixty-eight. He's scared, I think, though he'd never say it. I didn't know what to do with that, so I fixed the printer. Well, I plugged it in.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: How's your energy been, a few weeks on from stopping the medication?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Lumpy. Some good days. Some days I'm all tabs and no output. I've gone back to the ramen site, I'm reviewing places at one in the morning again. Eleven noodle shops this month. I'm their top contributor.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: (smiles) Top contributor. What usually comes just before the reviewing starts?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Something at work I'm avoiding. Right now it's a database migration that's been mine for a month. Every time I start it I find something else to tidy. Yesterday I changed my desktop wallpaper to a plain colour. That took forty minutes.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: What feels risky about the migration?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: If I get it wrong it's very public. Everyone sees the alerts go off. Everyone knows whose name is on it.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Everyone sees. Being seen getting it wrong.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yeah. I know where that comes from, I don't need to go there today. Can I tell you about the bus app instead? It has eleven users now. One of them left a five-star rating that just says 'finally'.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Eleven users. That's lovely.

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: It's the most validated I've felt in months. From a stranger. About a bus. I'm choosing not to examine that.

turns.speaker: therapist
turns.text: Let's hold onto it anyway. Same time in two weeks?

turns.speaker: client
turns.text: Yes. I'll try to have a less lumpy fortnight. No promises about the noodle reviews.

queries.query: Priya left about fifteen notes on my code review on Tuesday. All fair, honestly, nothing nasty. I shut the laptop and didn't open it again until Thursday, and told the team I had a migraine.

chain.fact: After his father's verdicts he would switch off for hours, lying under his desk.
His father read his school reports aloud at the dinner table: 'if you just applied yourself'.

queries.reasoning: Fair written feedback on his work is the same trigger as the dinner-table reports, and shutting the laptop for two days is the adult version of switching off under the desk.
queries.why_it_matters: Treated as procrastination or a time-management slip, the therapist misses the shame response to evaluation that drives it.

queries.query: The Captain's put a 'quick chat about the half-year' in my calendar for Thursday, no agenda. I've already drafted my resignation in my head three times.

chain.fact: 'The Captain' is his private nickname for his manager Ruth.
Ruth is the best manager he has had; she set up his accommodations and backs him.

queries.reasoning: The Captain is Ruth, whose track record is supportive, so the leap to resignation comes from his shame template, not from anything she has done.
queries.why_it_matters: Without resolving the nickname the therapist can't test his catastrophic prediction against the evidence that this manager is on his side.

queries.query: Honestly, nothing works. I've tried the timer thing, the apps, cold showers, journaling, all of it. My head is just loud all the time and I'm sick of it.

chain.fact: He stopped bouldering about a month before late June; the membership lapsed.
Bouldering made his mind completely quiet and helped him sleep.

queries.reasoning: Something did work: climbing quieted his mind, and it lapsed around the time things got worse, so 'nothing works' leaves out a proven resource.
queries.why_it_matters: The therapist might add yet another technique instead of helping him get back to the one activity that clearly helped.

queries.query: My focus has been shocking. On Monday I sat down to do a two-hour ticket, and four hours later I'd reorganised all my config files and read the entire history of submarines. Is this just who I am?

chain.fact: He stopped the stimulant in mid-June because of appetite loss and insomnia.
On the medication his attention improved markedly (wrote a design doc in one sitting).
He started a long-acting stimulant in early May.

queries.reasoning: His current state is off medication after a trial that worked but had side effects, so the drop in attention is expected and the GP's offer of another option is relevant.
